summary: Vasopressor used to raise blood pressure in adults with severe, acute hypotension. Nursing focus: infusion-site and tissue protection, avoiding abrupt interruption, and rhythm and pressure monitoring.

items.text: The label describes norepinephrine as a catecholamine indicated to raise blood pressure in adults with severe, acute hypotension.

In adult septic shock, SSC 2026 prioritizes norepinephrine as the initial vasopressor in most patients. With concomitant cardiac dysfunction, either norepinephrine or epinephrine is a conditional option with very low certainty; the team considers rhythm and perfusion.
The label advises infusing into a large vein, because extravasation can cause local tissue necrosis through vasoconstriction.
Check the infusion site and surrounding tissue for signs of extravasation or ischaemia, and report them at once.

Avoid unnecessary interruptions of a functioning norepinephrine infusion because abrupt cessation can cause marked hypotension. **If extravasation is suspected, do not continue infusing through the compromised catheter**: stop delivery at that site, assess and urgently escalate, and coordinate safe alternative access to maintain ordered haemodynamic support under the local emergency protocol.
Frequency of blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm checks follows the unit's vasoactive infusion protocol.
Check the infusion site frequently for free flow and watch for signs of extravasation; the label advises infusing into a large vein.
The label calls for cardiac monitoring in patients with underlying heart disease or arrhythmias, and for watching the skin of the extremities in susceptible patients.

During peripheral use, inspect the access site and surrounding skin for pain, swelling, pallor or blanching and any change in patency; apply the organisation's documented frequency and escalation pathway rather than assuming one universal safe duration or access location.

Escalating vasopressor requirements, multiple agents or unreliable repeated cuff measurements warrant assessment for invasive arterial pressure monitoring. Assess capillary refill and ordered serial lactate together with other perfusion findings.
Tissue ischaemia: avoid extravasation into the tissues because local necrosis can follow; management of an extravasation, including any infiltration treatment, is a prescriber or protocol decision.
Sudden cessation of the infusion may cause marked hypotension (label warning).
Cardiac arrhythmias and allergic reactions are listed among the label's warnings and precautions.

A restored blood pressure does not exclude poor organ perfusion, especially when circulating volume is inadequate. Escalate suspected hypovolaemia and ongoing perfusion deficits for clinician assessment.
The label lists tissue ischaemia, hypotension after abrupt discontinuation and cardiac arrhythmias as the serious adverse reactions described in its warnings.

The most common adverse reactions are hypertension and bradycardia; the label also lists ischaemic injury, anxiety, transient headache, respiratory difficulty and pulmonary oedema, and extravasation necrosis at the injection site.

Suspected peripheral extravasation is an exception to avoiding unnecessary interruption: stop delivery through the affected cannula, call the responsible team and pharmacy immediately, assess haemodynamic status and site changes, and arrange clinician-directed alternative vascular access for essential vasopressor support. Do not force-flush or automatically remove the catheter before the unit's extravasation procedure is followed.
Escalate promptly for suspected extravasation, new arrhythmia, falling blood pressure or an interrupted infusion.

Use the unit's early warning score (for example, the Royal College of Physicians' NEWS2 track-and-trigger system) to standardise recognition of acute deterioration: a medium aggregate score is a key trigger for an urgent clinical review, and a high aggregate score triggers an emergency clinical response. This is a generic nursing escalation framework, not specific to this medicine; it does not replace this medicine's own escalation triggers, which remain local protocol.
Record the infusion site checks, haemodynamic readings, pump checks and escalation per unit standard.
Use a structured handover (SBAR) when escalating.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Inspect the infusion site and surrounding skin for blanching, coolness or swelling.
Monitor blood pressure, heart rate and rhythm at the unit's frequency.

Avoid unintended interruption of essential support. If extravasation is suspected, stop delivery through the affected catheter and urgently coordinate safe alternative access under the local procedure.
Report suspected extravasation, arrhythmia or falling pressure immediately.
Record site checks, pump checks and responses.
Assess perfusion trends, including urine output, skin findings and ordered lactate results; escalate persistent hypoperfusion even if the measured pressure has improved.
